PROP
43
LIMITS VOTERS’ ABILITY TO RAISE REVENUES FOR LOCAL GOVERNMENT SERVICES. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by the Legislature
Limits voters’ ability to pass voter-proposed local special taxes by increasing percentage of votes needed to approve such ballot measures from a majority (over 50%) to two-thirds, beginning January 1, 2027. Fiscal Impact: Possibility that local government tax revenues will not go up as much in the future due to a higher vote threshold for certain taxes. Supporters: California Taxpayers Association; Family Business Association of California; California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce Opponents: California Professional Firefighters; California Federation of Teachers; Nurse Alliance of SEIU CA.
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: Certain local government taxes would require two-thirds approval by voters.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: Certain local government taxes could continue to be approved by voters with a majority vote.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Prop. 43 protects taxpayers by restoring Proposition 13’s two-thirds vote requirement to pass local special taxes, including sales taxes, real estate taxes and utility taxes. Courts have allowed special interests to pass earmarked tax increases with fewer votes. Prop. 43 closes this loophole, protecting taxpayers, homeowners and renters. Vote yes.
CON
PROPOSITION 43 LIMITS VOTERS’ ABILITY TO FUND ESSENTIAL LOCAL SERVICES including fire protection, 911 response, schools, roads, hospitals and affordable housing. It doesn’t cut your taxes and lets just 33.4% of voters veto what nearly 67% want. Protect your vote and majority rule. Vote NO on Proposition 43.

# Proposition 43
Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services.
Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
## Analysis of Measure
### Background
***Vote Thresholds for Local Taxes.*** The State Constitution allows local governments to increase taxes with local voter approval.
Tax increases can be put on a ballot by voters or a local governing board (such as a city council or board of supervisors).
Increases in some types of local taxes require a two-thirds vote to approve them, while other types of taxes require a majority (more than half) vote to approve them.
Some local tax increases are approved permanently, while others are approved for a limited period of time.
Before those taxes expire, voters can be asked whether to extend them.
### Proposal
***Requires Certain Local Taxes Receive Two-Thirds Approval by Voters.*** Under current law, local taxes that are used for a specific purpose require a two-thirds vote to be approved.
These are called special taxes.
However, recent court decisions have allowed special taxes that are *proposed by voters* to be approved with a majority vote.
Under Proposition 43, beginning on January 1, 2027, any new, increased, or extended local special taxes proposed by voters would require a two-thirds vote.

## Prop. 43: Make it Harder to Pass Special Taxes for Cities and Counties
**How they’re selling it:** It’s too easy for special interest groups to raise taxes.
**In plain English:** California has long had a law that required special taxes (like a hotel room-tax increase or a sales-tax increase to build a stadium or any specific goal) to be approved by two-thirds of voters.
But years ago, a California Supreme Court ruling effectively exempted citizens initiatives from this threshold.
Since then, supporters of new taxes for special purposes have been able to collect signatures and support campaigns to pass taxes sometimes without the explicit support of the government that would collect them.
But those independent initiatives only need support from a majority of voters to pass.
This proposition would close that loophole.
If you think all taxes to support special projects or goals in a city or county should have to earn the support of two-thirds of voters to be implemented, vote yes.
If you think the status quo is fine where independent groups can collect signatures and put a special tax on the ballot and a majority of voters is all it should need to pass, vote no.

PROP
43
LIMITS VOTERS’ ABILITY TO RAISE REVENUES FOR LOCAL GOVERNMENT SERVICES. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by the Legislature
Limits voters’ ability to pass voter-proposed local special taxes by increasing percentage of votes needed to approve such ballot measures from a majority (over 50%) to two-thirds, beginning January 1, 2027. Fiscal Impact: Possibility that local government tax revenues will not go up as much in the future due to a higher vote threshold for certain taxes. Supporters: California Taxpayers Association; Family Business Association of California; California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce Opponents: California Professional Firefighters; California Federation of Teachers; Nurse Alliance of SEIU CA.
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: Certain local government taxes would require two-thirds approval by voters.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: Certain local government taxes could continue to be approved by voters with a majority vote.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Prop. 43 protects taxpayers by restoring Proposition 13’s two-thirds vote requirement to pass local special taxes, including sales taxes, real estate taxes and utility taxes. Courts have allowed special interests to pass earmarked tax increases with fewer votes. Prop. 43 closes this loophole, protecting taxpayers, homeowners and renters. Vote yes.
CON
PROPOSITION 43 LIMITS VOTERS’ ABILITY TO FUND ESSENTIAL LOCAL SERVICES including fire protection, 911 response, schools, roads, hospitals and affordable housing. It doesn’t cut your taxes and lets just 33.4% of voters veto what nearly 67% want. Protect your vote and majority rule. Vote NO on Proposition 43.

Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services.
Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
## Analysis of Measure
### Background
***Vote Thresholds for Local Taxes.*** The State Constitution allows local governments to increase taxes with local voter approval.
Tax increases can be put on a ballot by voters or a local governing board (such as a city council or board of supervisors).
Increases in some types of local taxes require a two-thirds vote to approve them, while other types of taxes require a majority (more than half) vote to approve them.
Some local tax increases are approved permanently, while others are approved for a limited period of time.
Before those taxes expire, voters can be asked whether to extend them.
### Proposal
***Requires Certain Local Taxes Receive Two-Thirds Approval by Voters.*** Under current law, local taxes that are used for a specific purpose require a two-thirds vote to be approved.
These are called special taxes.
However, recent court decisions have allowed special taxes that are *proposed by voters* to be approved with a majority vote.
Under Proposition 43, beginning on January 1, 2027, any new, increased, or extended local special taxes proposed by voters would require a two-thirds vote.

## Prop. 43: Make it Harder to Pass Special Taxes for Cities and Counties
**How they’re selling it:** It’s too easy for special interest groups to raise taxes.
**In plain English:** California has long had a law that required special taxes (like a hotel room-tax increase or a sales-tax increase to build a stadium or any specific goal) to be approved by two-thirds of voters.
But years ago, a California Supreme Court ruling effectively exempted citizens initiatives from this threshold.
Since then, supporters of new taxes for special purposes have been able to collect signatures and support campaigns to pass taxes sometimes without the explicit support of the government that would collect them.
But those independent initiatives only need support from a majority of voters to pass.
This proposition would close that loophole.
If you think all taxes to support special projects or goals in a city or county should have to earn the support of two-thirds of voters to be implemented, vote yes.
If you think the status quo is fine where independent groups can collect signatures and put a special tax on the ballot and a majority of voters is all it should need to pass, vote no.

Put on the Ballot by the Legislature

# 2026 California Proposition 43
**Proposition 43** is a proposed legislative constitutional amendment on the November 3, 2026, ballot in California.
Starting on January 1, 2027, Proposition 43 would restore the two-thirds voter approval requirement to impose, extend, or increase a local special (legally dedicated) tax under Proposition 13 for any proposed special tax that qualifies for the ballot under the local initiative power.^[1]^ Proposition 43 would also prohibit local governments, including under the local initiative power, from imposing additional ad valorem taxes on real property (taxes based on the assessed value of property), except as otherwise allowed under the California Constitution.^[2]^

# 2026 California Proposition 43
**Proposition 43** is a proposed legislative constitutional amendment on the November 3, 2026, ballot in California.
Starting on January 1, 2027, Proposition 43 would restore the two-thirds voter approval requirement to impose, extend, or increase a local special (legally dedicated) tax under Proposition 13 for any proposed special tax that qualifies for the ballot under the local initiative power.^[1]^ Proposition 43 would also prohibit local governments, including under the local initiative power, from imposing additional ad valorem taxes on real property (taxes based on the assessed value of property), except as otherwise allowed under the California Constitution.^[2]^
Proposition 43 was proposed to overturn appellate court rulings following the 2017 *Upland* decision by the California Supreme Court,^[3]^ which created a distinction between taxes proposed by the governing body of a local government and taxes proposed under the local initiative power for purposes of applying the two-thirds voter approval requirement for special taxes under Proposition 13.
These appellate court rulings held that citizen-led special tax proposals under the local initiative power were no longer subject to the two-thirds voter approval requirement under Proposition 13.

2026 elections: Track results for all 14 California propositions
This November, California voters will make choices on a variety of issues — from housing to elections, healthcare and taxes.
Ashley Zavala (https://www.kcra.com/news-team/21271fb1-6e06-4bcf-8b56-97b158a0e14b)

Nijzel Dotson
Digital Producer
There are 14 propositions on the General Election ballot (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/).
Five of the measures are related to taxes, three are related to elections and campaigns, three ask voters to borrow money for specific issues, and three make changes to state laws around spending, saving and environmentally related construction rules.
Advertisement
See live Election Day updates here (https://www.kcra.com/article/california-election-day-live-updates-nov-3/74317260)
Track full election results here (http://www.kcra.com/article/california-election-night-results-2026/74184627)
You can track the results below after polls close at 8 p.m.
PROPOSITION 1
If passed, Proposition 1, also known as the Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026, would approve $11.25 billion for low-income families, farmworkers, students, foster youth and veterans.
See Prop. 1 results:
PROPOSITION 2
Proposition 2 would double the cap on the state’s rainy day fund from 10% to 20% of annual tax revenue.
California’s rainy day fund, approved by voters more than two decades ago, has helped the state navigate financial challenges, including the pandemic and budget shortfalls, while protecting funding for schools, public safety and other critical services.
See Prop. 2 results:
PROPOSITION 3
California voters will decide whether to make a temporary higher state income tax on California's wealthiest taxpayers permanent. It's on this year's ballot as Proposition 3 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/index.htm).
Voters first approved the temporary tax in 2012 (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2012/30_11_2012.aspx). It was renewed in 2016 (https://www.lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=55&year=2016). It's currently set to expire in 2031.
See Prop. 3 results:
PROPOSITION 4
Proposition 4 would allow cities and counties to set up public campaign financing. For those that do, politicians in that area can use the money for their campaigns as long as they meet certain thresholds.
See Prop. 4 results:
PROPOSITION 5
Proposition 5 would limit recall ballots to just one yes-or-no question: Should an elected official be recalled from office?
Currently, recall ballots also have a second section where voters are asked to choose a successor if the recall passes. Prop 5 would eliminate that second section. If the recall passes, a new leader is chosen later in a separate process.
See Prop. 5 results:
PROPOSITION 37
Proposition 37 proposes a $25 billion loan program to help California residents overcome the challenge of affording down payments on new homes.
The measure (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37.pdf), authored by former state Senate Majority Leader and California Assembly Speaker Bob Hertzberg, would allow the state government to issue bonds to help residents borrow up to 17% of their down payment, requiring them to contribute at least 3% themselves, while their primary mortgage would cover the remaining 80%.
See Prop. 37 results:
PROPOSITION 38
Prop 38 would direct the state to issue $8.4 billion in bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research, which includes research on diseases such as cancer, Parkinson's, ALS and MS.
See Prop. 38 results:
PROPOSITION 39
Proposition 39 requires government-issued ID at the polls or the last four digits of the ID number for mail-in ballots. Elections officials would also be required to annually report the percentage of voters with verified citizenship.
See Prop. 39 results:
PROPOSITION 40
Proposition 40 asks voters to approve a one-time, 5% tax on the assets of California residents with a net worth of a billion dollars with the goal of raising $100 billion to fund mostly healthcare programs.
See Prop. 40 results:
PROPOSITION 41
Proposition 41 is in response to the proposed billionaire tax, requiring strict oversight of how new taxes are used and prohibiting any new taxes that are exempted from the state’s spending limit required under the state constitution, meaning it would cancel out the billionaire tax. The measure with the most votes becomes law.
See Prop. 41 results:
PROPOSITION 42
Proposition 42 would ban new state taxes on personal property and assets, including retirement accounts, personal savings, and investments.
If the billionaire tax through Prop 40 and either Proposition 41 or 42 pass, the measure with the most votes will become law.
See Prop. 42 results:
PROPOSITION 43
Proposition 43 would make it more difficult to pass new special taxes in cities and counties. Currently, local governments such as city councils or county supervisors can propose special taxes, which require approval by a two-thirds vote from residents. However, special taxes proposed by citizens or special interest groups only need a simple majority to pass.
See Prop. 43 results:
PROPOSITION 44
Proposition 44 aims at changing how community health clinics spend taxpayer dollars. Supporters say it will increase accountability, but opponents warn it could threaten services patients rely on.
See Prop. 44 results:
PROPOSITION 45
Proposition 45 would change parts of California's Environmental Quality Act to speed up environmental review of housing, transportation and other infrastructure projects. It would also limit the ability of lawsuits to stop or slow a project.
See Prop. 45 results:

Proposition 43
Raise vote threshold for special tax measures
This would make it harder to impose or increase local taxes by raising the threshold for local citizen-driven special tax ballot initiatives to pass from a simple majority to two-thirds. The two-thirds threshold already applies to taxes proposed by local governments but not by individuals. The measure reflects a deal between state lawmakers and the anti-tax Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association to keep a more restrictive tax proposal off the ballot.

Proposition committees
These committees are primarily formed to campaign for or against a proposition. They must identify contributors who give $100 or more, or loan a committee money. There are no limits on how much contributors can give or loan. Contributors who had their loans repaid or forgiven are still included. We exclude contributors who gave less than $100 in total. Contributors who made loans as part or all of their total are identified with an asterisk (*).
For funding by industry, we used existing sources, traditional machine learning and large language models to help categorize contributors who gave $5,000 or more in total, with CalMatters journalists reviewing the results. We also categorized the donors of political action committees that contributed to a campaign and used the results to calculate which industries should be applied. Major donors include individuals who self-identified as retired, self-employed, unemployed, a homemaker or a student.

Outside spending
Separate from proposition committees, outside groups can pay for ads, mailers and other efforts to influence voters. They can’t coordinate that spending with proposition committees. There is no limit on how much they can spend.

LIMITS VOTERS’ ABILITY TO RAISE REVENUES FOR LOCAL GOVERNMENT SERVICES. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT. Limits voters’ ability to pass voter-proposed local special taxes by increasing percentage of votes needed to approve such ballot measures from a majority (over 50%) to two-thirds, beginning January 1, 2027. Fiscal Impact: Possibility that local government tax revenues will not go up as much in the future due to a higher vote threshold for certain taxes.

2026 elections: Track results for all 14 California propositions
This November, California voters will make choices on a variety of issues — from housing to elections, healthcare and taxes.
Ashley Zavala (https://www.kcra.com/news-team/21271fb1-6e06-4bcf-8b56-97b158a0e14b)
Political Director (https://www.kcra.com/news-team/21271fb1-6e06-4bcf-8b56-97b158a0e14b)
Nijzel Dotson
Digital Producer
There are 14 propositions on the General Election ballot (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/).
Five of the measures are related to taxes, three are related to elections and campaigns, three ask voters to borrow money for specific issues, and three make changes to state laws around spending, saving and environmentally related construction rules.
Advertisement
See live Election Day updates here (https://www.kcra.com/article/california-election-day-live-updates-nov-3/74317260)
Track full election results here (http://www.kcra.com/article/california-election-night-results-2026/74184627)
You can track the results below after polls close at 8 p.m.
PROPOSITION 1
If passed, Proposition 1, also known as the Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026, would approve $11.25 billion for low-income families, farmworkers, students, foster youth and veterans.
See Prop. 1 results:
PROPOSITION 2
Proposition 2 would double the cap on the state’s rainy day fund from 10% to 20% of annual tax revenue.
California’s rainy day fund, approved by voters more than two decades ago, has helped the state navigate financial challenges, including the pandemic and budget shortfalls, while protecting funding for schools, public safety and other critical services.
See Prop. 2 results:
PROPOSITION 3
California voters will decide whether to make a temporary higher state income tax on California's wealthiest taxpayers permanent. It's on this year's ballot as Proposition 3 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/index.htm).
Voters first approved the temporary tax in 2012 (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2012/30_11_2012.aspx). It was renewed in 2016 (https://www.lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=55&year=2016). It's currently set to expire in 2031.
See Prop. 3 results:
PROPOSITION 4
Proposition 4 would allow cities and counties to set up public campaign financing. For those that do, politicians in that area can use the money for their campaigns as long as they meet certain thresholds.
See Prop. 4 results:
PROPOSITION 5
Proposition 5 would limit recall ballots to just one yes-or-no question: Should an elected official be recalled from office?
Currently, recall ballots also have a second section where voters are asked to choose a successor if the recall passes. Prop 5 would eliminate that second section. If the recall passes, a new leader is chosen later in a separate process.
See Prop. 5 results:
PROPOSITION 37
Proposition 37 proposes a $25 billion loan program to help California residents overcome the challenge of affording down payments on new homes.
The measure (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37.pdf), authored by former state Senate Majority Leader and California Assembly Speaker Bob Hertzberg, would allow the state government to issue bonds to help residents borrow up to 17% of their down payment, requiring them to contribute at least 3% themselves, while their primary mortgage would cover the remaining 80%.
See Prop. 37 results:
PROPOSITION 38
Prop 38 would direct the state to issue $8.4 billion in bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research, which includes research on diseases such as cancer, Parkinson's, ALS and MS.
See Prop. 38 results:
PROPOSITION 39
Proposition 39 requires government-issued ID at the polls or the last four digits of the ID number for mail-in ballots. Elections officials would also be required to annually report the percentage of voters with verified citizenship.
See Prop. 39 results:
PROPOSITION 40
Proposition 40 asks voters to approve a one-time, 5% tax on the assets of California residents with a net worth of a billion dollars with the goal of raising $100 billion to fund mostly healthcare programs.
See Prop. 40 results:
PROPOSITION 41
Proposition 41 is in response to the proposed billionaire tax, requiring strict oversight of how new taxes are used and prohibiting any new taxes that are exempted from the state’s spending limit required under the state constitution, meaning it would cancel out the billionaire tax. The measure with the most votes becomes law.
See Prop. 41 results:
PROPOSITION 42
Proposition 42 would ban new state taxes on personal property and assets, including retirement accounts, personal savings, and investments.
If the billionaire tax through Prop 40 and either Proposition 41 or 42 pass, the measure with the most votes will become law.
See Prop. 42 results:
PROPOSITION 43
Proposition 43 would make it more difficult to pass new special taxes in cities and counties. Currently, local governments such as city councils or county supervisors can propose special taxes, which require approval by a two-thirds vote from residents. However, special taxes proposed by citizens or special interest groups only need a simple majority to pass.
See Prop. 43 results:
PROPOSITION 44
Proposition 44 aims at changing how community health clinics spend taxpayer dollars. Supporters say it will increase accountability, but opponents warn it could threaten services patients rely on.
See Prop. 44 results:
PROPOSITION 45
Proposition 45 would change parts of California's Environmental Quality Act to speed up environmental review of housing, transportation and other infrastructure projects. It would also limit the ability of lawsuits to stop or slow a project.
See Prop. 45 results:

2026 elections: Track results for all 14 California propositions
This November, California voters will make choices on a variety of issues — from housing to elections, healthcare and taxes.
Ashley Zavala (https://www.kcra.com/news-team/21271fb1-6e06-4bcf-8b56-97b158a0e14b)
Political Director (https://www.kcra.com/news-team/21271fb1-6e06-4bcf-8b56-97b158a0e14b)
Nijzel Dotson
Digital Producer
There are 14 propositions on the General Election ballot (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/).
Five of the measures are related to taxes, three are related to elections and campaigns, three ask voters to borrow money for specific issues, and three make changes to state laws around spending, saving and environmentally related construction rules.
Advertisement
See live Election Day updates here (https://www.kcra.com/article/california-election-day-live-updates-nov-3/74317260)
Track full election results here (http://www.kcra.com/article/california-election-night-results-2026/74184627)
You can track the results below after polls close at 8 p.m.
PROPOSITION 1
If passed, Proposition 1, also known as the Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026, would approve $11.25 billion for low-income families, farmworkers, students, foster youth and veterans.
See Prop. 1 results:
PROPOSITION 2
Proposition 2 would double the cap on the state’s rainy day fund from 10% to 20% of annual tax revenue.
California’s rainy day fund, approved by voters more than two decades ago, has helped the state navigate financial challenges, including the pandemic and budget shortfalls, while protecting funding for schools, public safety and other critical services.
See Prop. 2 results:
PROPOSITION 3
California voters will decide whether to make a temporary higher state income tax on California's wealthiest taxpayers permanent. It's on this year's ballot as Proposition 3 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/index.htm).
Voters first approved the temporary tax in 2012 (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2012/30_11_2012.aspx). It was renewed in 2016 (https://www.lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=55&year=2016). It's currently set to expire in 2031.
See Prop. 3 results:
PROPOSITION 4
Proposition 4 would allow cities and counties to set up public campaign financing. For those that do, politicians in that area can use the money for their campaigns as long as they meet certain thresholds.
See Prop. 4 results:
PROPOSITION 5
Proposition 5 would limit recall ballots to just one yes-or-no question: Should an elected official be recalled from office?
Currently, recall ballots also have a second section where voters are asked to choose a successor if the recall passes. Prop 5 would eliminate that second section. If the recall passes, a new leader is chosen later in a separate process.
See Prop. 5 results:
PROPOSITION 37
Proposition 37 proposes a $25 billion loan program to help California residents overcome the challenge of affording down payments on new homes.
The measure (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37.pdf), authored by former state Senate Majority Leader and California Assembly Speaker Bob Hertzberg, would allow the state government to issue bonds to help residents borrow up to 17% of their down payment, requiring them to contribute at least 3% themselves, while their primary mortgage would cover the remaining 80%.
See Prop. 37 results:
PROPOSITION 38
Prop 38 would direct the state to issue $8.4 billion in bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research, which includes research on diseases such as cancer, Parkinson's, ALS and MS.
See Prop. 38 results:
PROPOSITION 39
Proposition 39 requires government-issued ID at the polls or the last four digits of the ID number for mail-in ballots. Elections officials would also be required to annually report the percentage of voters with verified citizenship.
See Prop. 39 results:
PROPOSITION 40
Proposition 40 asks voters to approve a one-time, 5% tax on the assets of California residents with a net worth of a billion dollars with the goal of raising $100 billion to fund mostly healthcare programs.
See Prop. 40 results:
PROPOSITION 41
Proposition 41 is in response to the proposed billionaire tax, requiring strict oversight of how new taxes are used and prohibiting any new taxes that are exempted from the state’s spending limit required under the state constitution, meaning it would cancel out the billionaire tax. The measure with the most votes becomes law.
See Prop. 41 results:
PROPOSITION 42
Proposition 42 would ban new state taxes on personal property and assets, including retirement accounts, personal savings, and investments.

PROPOSITION 43
Proposition 43 would make it more difficult to pass new special taxes in cities and counties. Currently, local governments such as city councils or county supervisors can propose special taxes, which require approval by a two-thirds vote from residents. However, special taxes proposed by citizens or special interest groups only need a simple majority to pass.

Proposition 44 aims at changing how community health clinics spend taxpayer dollars. Supporters say it will increase accountability, but opponents warn it could threaten services patients rely on.

Proposition 43
Raise vote threshold for special tax measures
This would make it harder to impose or increase local taxes by raising the threshold for local citizen-driven special tax ballot initiatives to pass from a simple majority to two-thirds. The two-thirds threshold already applies to taxes proposed by local governments but not by individuals. The measure reflects a deal between state lawmakers and the anti-tax Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association to keep a more restrictive tax proposal off the ballot.

Proposition committees
These committees are primarily formed to campaign for or against a proposition. They must identify contributors who give $100 or more, or loan a committee money. There are no limits on how much contributors can give or loan. Contributors who had their loans repaid or forgiven are still included. We exclude contributors who gave less than $100 in total. Contributors who made loans as part or all of their total are identified with an asterisk (*).
For funding by industry, we used existing sources, traditional machine learning and large language models to help categorize contributors who gave $5,000 or more in total, with CalMatters journalists reviewing the results. We also categorized the donors of political action committees that contributed to a campaign and used the results to calculate which industries should be applied. Major donors include individuals who self-identified as retired, self-employed, unemployed, a homemaker or a student.

I'm noting there's also the Prop 40 billionaire tax and other tax measures, so the ballot may be crowded with confusing tax questions. Next I'll check whether election results are already posted, searching for Prop 43 results and whether it passes or fails.

By Gordon M. Webster Jr. (https://thebusinessjournal.com/byline/gordon-m-webster-jr/) | October 27, 2026 - 9:24 AM
Share:
Does it matter who writes a tax?
Under Proposition 13, a local special tax, meaning one earmarked for a specific purpose, needs two-thirds of voters to pass. City councils, county boards and special districts all live with that rule.
Then came 2017. In California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland , the state Supreme Court ruled on a narrow question about election timing for citizen initiatives. Lower courts read the decision more broadly. The result: Special taxes placed on the ballot by petition could pass with 50% plus one.
Fresno saw it play out. Measure P, the 2018 parks sales tax, drew 52.17% of the vote. The city treated it as defeated, and a Fresno County judge agreed. An appeals court reversed that ruling and held that a simple majority was enough.
Proposition 43 closes that gap. Beginning Jan. 1, 2027, any new, increased or extended local special tax proposed by voters would need two-thirds approval. That is the same bar local governments already clear.
What it does not do:
Repeal any tax already on the books.
Change the threshold for general taxes.
Cap real estate transfer taxes.
That last item was part of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association’s original initiative. It was dropped in a June deal with the governor’s office and legislative leaders. Lawmakers placed the narrower compromise, ACA 22, on the ballot by votes of 35-1 in the Senate and 68-2 in the Assembly.
Why should employers pay attention?
Special taxes land on business: sales taxes, parcel taxes and gross receipts taxes. Supporters argue that special interests have used the simple-majority path to pass earmarked taxes in low-turnout elections. Backers include the California Taxpayers Association, the Family Business Association of California and the California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce.
Opponents see it differently. The California Professional Firefighters, the California Federation of Teachers and SEIU’s Nurse Alliance argue the measure lets one-third of voters block funding for fire protection, schools and housing.
The race is close. A September Public Policy Institute of California survey found 51% of likely voters opposed and 43% in favor, CalMatters reported.
The Business Journal will weigh in on Prop. 43 and other measures affecting business in this Friday’s issue.
Ballots are already in mailboxes. Vote-by-mail ballots must be postmarked by Nov. 3.
The question on the ballot is simple: How many of your neighbors should have to agree before a new tax becomes law?

Gordon Webster, Jr. (https://thebusinessjournal.com/news/blogs/gordon-webster-jr/) Prop. 43 asks who should clear the two-thirds bar on local taxes
By Gordon M. Webster Jr. (https://thebusinessjournal.com/byline/gordon-m-webster-jr/) | October 27, 2026 - 9:24 AM
Share:
Does it matter who writes a tax?
Under Proposition 13, a local special tax, meaning one earmarked for a specific purpose, needs two-thirds of voters to pass. City councils, county boards and special districts all live with that rule.
Then came 2017. In California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland , the state Supreme Court ruled on a narrow question about election timing for citizen initiatives. Lower courts read the decision more broadly. The result: Special taxes placed on the ballot by petition could pass with 50% plus one.
Fresno saw it play out. Measure P, the 2018 parks sales tax, drew 52.17% of the vote. The city treated it as defeated, and a Fresno County judge agreed. An appeals court reversed that ruling and held that a simple majority was enough.
Proposition 43 closes that gap. Beginning Jan. 1, 2027, any new, increased or extended local special tax proposed by voters would need two-thirds approval. That is the same bar local governments already clear.
What it does not do:
Repeal any tax already on the books.
Change the threshold for general taxes.
Cap real estate transfer taxes.
That last item was part of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association’s original initiative. It was dropped in a June deal with the governor’s office and legislative leaders. Lawmakers placed the narrower compromise, ACA 22, on the ballot by votes of 35-1 in the Senate and 68-2 in the Assembly.
Why should employers pay attention?
Special taxes land on business: sales taxes, parcel taxes and gross receipts taxes. Supporters argue that special interests have used the simple-majority path to pass earmarked taxes in low-turnout elections. Backers include the California Taxpayers Association, the Family Business Association of California and the California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce.
Opponents see it differently. The California Professional Firefighters, the California Federation of Teachers and SEIU’s Nurse Alliance argue the measure lets one-third of voters block funding for fire protection, schools and housing.
The race is close. A September Public Policy Institute of California survey found 51% of likely voters opposed and 43% in favor, CalMatters reported.
The Business Journal will weigh in on Prop. 43 and other measures affecting business in this Friday’s issue.
Ballots are already in mailboxes. Vote-by-mail ballots must be postmarked by Nov. 3.
The question on the ballot is simple: How many of your neighbors should have to agree before a new tax becomes law?

Under Proposition 13, a local special tax, meaning one earmarked for a specific purpose, needs two-thirds of voters to pass. City councils, county boards and special districts all live with that rule.
Then came 2017. In California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland , the state Supreme Court ruled on a narrow question about election timing for citizen initiatives. Lower courts read the decision more broadly. The result: Special taxes placed on the ballot by petition could pass with 50% plus one.
Fresno saw it play out. Measure P, the 2018 parks sales tax, drew 52.17% of the vote. The city treated it as defeated, and a Fresno County judge agreed. An appeals court reversed that ruling and held that a simple majority was enough.
Proposition 43 closes that gap. Beginning Jan. 1, 2027, any new, increased or extended local special tax proposed by voters would need two-thirds approval. That is the same bar local governments already clear.
What it does not do:
Repeal any tax already on the books.
Change the threshold for general taxes.
Cap real estate transfer taxes.
That last item was part of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association’s original initiative. It was dropped in a June deal with the governor’s office and legislative leaders. Lawmakers placed the narrower compromise, ACA 22, on the ballot by votes of 35-1 in the Senate and 68-2 in the Assembly.
Why should employers pay attention?
Special taxes land on business: sales taxes, parcel taxes and gross receipts taxes. Supporters argue that special interests have used the simple-majority path to pass earmarked taxes in low-turnout elections. Backers include the California Taxpayers Association, the Family Business Association of California and the California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce.
Opponents see it differently. The California Professional Firefighters, the California Federation of Teachers and SEIU’s Nurse Alliance argue the measure lets one-third of voters block funding for fire protection, schools and housing.
The race is close. A September Public Policy Institute of California survey found 51% of likely voters opposed and 43% in favor, CalMatters reported.
The Business Journal will weigh in on Prop. 43 and other measures affecting business in this Friday’s issue.
Ballots are already in mailboxes. Vote-by-mail ballots must be postmarked by Nov. 3.
The question on the ballot is simple: How many of your neighbors should have to agree before a new tax becomes law?

Schaben, Los Angeles Times via Getty Images In summary The measure would require two-thirds of voters to approve any local special taxes, instead of the simple majority for citizen-led initiatives. Anti-tax advocates say it should be that hard for governments to tax Californians, but local officials say it could constrain funding for essential services. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. In 2022, 58% of Los Angeles city voters approved a hefty tax on mansion sales. In 2024, 62% of Sonoma County voters backed a half-cent sales tax to fund wildfire response and other emergency services. Neither would have become law under the threshold set by Proposition 43 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/), which would require a two-thirds vote to pass any local tax measures that pay for specific services. Anti-tax advocates such as the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, which helped get Prop. 43 on the ballot, say it should be harder (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/california-constitution-proposition-43-taxes/) to tax Californians in a state where tax rates are already high. They argue that the measure would apply an equal standard to whoever wants a special tax, whether the government or citizen groups. Californians voted in 1996 (https://lao.ca.gov/1996/120196_prop_218/understanding_prop218_1296.html) to establish a two-thirds threshold for special tax measures. For decades, it was widely assumed that the threshold applied to all special taxes — until 2017, when the state Supreme Court said (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2017/08/state-supreme-court-made-easier-raise-taxes/) the law specifically applied only to tax measures put on the ballot by local officials. But what about special taxes proposed by citizens? The court declined to clarify (https://calmatters.org/economy/2019/02/local-tax-chaos-california-supreme-court/). Confusion ensued. Since then, several high-profile local special tax measures placed on the ballot by nongovernmental groups have passed with a simple majority. Local government officials, labor unions and affordable housing advocates oppose the measure, arguing the proposal would make it difficult to collect revenues for essential services, such as firefighting, education and healthcare. They argue it would allow “minority rule (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/proposition-43-taxes-minority-rule/)” because it would only take a third of voters to block special taxes. Jon Coupal, president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, said Prop. 43 would clarify that the two-thirds rule applies to all special taxes. He said that the two-thirds vote requirement dates to the 1849 state Constitution, which required a supermajority vote of state lawmakers to ask voters to borrow money. “The power to tax is (the) government’s most draconian power,” he told CalMatters. “The people of the state of California have made it a policy that when you are going to exercise that power, it should require a higher degree of consensus.” But opponents say the initiative risks kneecapping funding for local services. Darrell Roberts, president of the California Professional Firefighters union, which represents 38,000 firefighters, called Prop. 43 an insurmountable roadblock (https://www.marinij.com/2026/10/03/opinion-prop-43-sacrifices-local-public-safety-to-protect-corporate-profits/) to raising money for community services. This November, Los Angeles voters will decide on a half-cent sales tax (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-06/lapd-union-will-oppose-half-cent-sales-tax-hike-pushed-by-firefighters-union) proposal to hire more firefighters, Roberts noted. “Under Prop. 43, it’s clear that the powerful few would be protected at the expense of everyone else,” he wrote in the Marin Independent Journal. Supporters have poured almost $15 million into the measure, nearly $10 million of it from the California Business Roundtable PAC. Opponents have collected $6 million, with the biggest contribution, $1.5 million, from a PAC affiliated with the Service Employees International Union of California. Sign up for free Δ Prop. 43 originated from L.A.’s ‘mansion tax’ fight Prop. 43 stems from a bitter fight over Los Angeles’ “mansion tax,” a 4% tax on real estate sales of more than $5.3 million and 5.5% on sales more than $10.6 million. The tax rates rise with inflation. It has generated $1.4 billion (https://housing.lacity.gov/ula-revenue) in revenue since it became law in 2023, according to the city. The tax angered real estate developers (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/04/proposition-realty-mansion-tax-jarvis/) and business groups, who said it impeded new construction of all kinds of developments, including affordable housing. The opposition fueled a campaign led by Coupal’s group earlier this year to qualify a ballot measure that would have slashed real estate sales taxes statewide, applied the two-thirds vote requirement to all special taxes and revoked taxes that previously passed by a simple majority, such as the mansion tax. Prop. 43 is a more modest proposal resulting from an eleventh-hour negotiation between Coupal and Democratic leaders in the state Legislature to kill the more extensive version. Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/buffy-wicks-165044), an Oakland Democrat, authored the compromise language (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260aca22). The measure is limited to the vote threshold and does not apply retroactively to taxes such as the mansion tax. Just days after the Legislature placed Prop. 43 on the ballot, Wicks said she is “adamantly opposed” to it. “The clock was running out, and we had a choice to make: Leave a retroactive measure on the ballot that threatened billions in local funding, or accept a much narrower constitutional amendment that I still believed was bad policy,” Wicks said (https://bsky.app/profile/buffywicks.bsky.social/post/3mpi3t4tkmp2h) in a social media post. Is there public appetite? This isn’t Coupal’s first rodeo. In 2024, his group sponsored a much broader ballot measure to make it harder to raise taxes, but the California Supreme Court unanimously blocked (https://calmatters.org/politics/2024/06/california-taxes-supreme-court-ballot/) it before the election, deeming it an illegal attempt to change the state’s constitution. How will a narrower Prop. 43 perform this year? A September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) from the nonpartisan Public Policy Institute of California found 51% of likely voters would vote no on Prop. 43, versus just 43% who would vote yes. But Coupal hopes the proposal taps into voters’ concerns about affordability and their frustration with the high cost of living in California. “We are in a general climate right now where Californians really feel overtaxed,” he said. “California needs to prioritize its spending before it asks for more.” READ NEXT Why are out-of-state billionaires funding a California voter ID measure? Schaben, Los Angeles Times via Getty Images In summary The measure would require two-thirds of voters to approve any local special taxes, instead of the simple majority for citizen-led initiatives. Anti-tax advocates say it should be that hard for governments to tax Californians, but local officials say it could constrain funding for essential services. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. In 2022, 58% of Los Angeles city voters approved a hefty tax on mansion sales. In 2024, 62% of Sonoma County voters backed a half-cent sales tax to fund wildfire response and other emergency services. Neither would have become law under the threshold set by Proposition 43 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/), which would require a two-thirds vote to pass any local tax measures that pay for specific services. Anti-tax advocates such as the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, which helped get Prop. 43 on the ballot, say it should be harder (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/california-constitution-proposition-43-taxes/) to tax Californians in a state where tax rates are already high. They argue that the measure would apply an equal standard to whoever wants a special tax, whether the government or citizen groups. Californians voted in 1996 (https://lao.ca.gov/1996/120196_prop_218/understanding_prop218_1296.html) to establish a two-thirds threshold for special tax measures. For decades, it was widely assumed that the threshold applied to all special taxes — until 2017, when the state Supreme Court said (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2017/08/state-supreme-court-made-easier-raise-taxes/) the law specifically applied only to tax measures put on the ballot by local officials. But what about special taxes proposed by citizens? The court declined to clarify (https://calmatters.org/economy/2019/02/local-tax-chaos-california-supreme-court/). Confusion ensued. Since then, several high-profile local special tax measures placed on the ballot by nongovernmental groups have passed with a simple majority. Local government officials, labor unions and affordable housing advocates oppose the measure, arguing the proposal would make it difficult to collect revenues for essential services, such as firefighting, education and healthcare. They argue it would allow “minority rule (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/proposition-43-taxes-minority-rule/)” because it would only take a third of voters to block special taxes. Jon Coupal, president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, said Prop. 43 would clarify that the two-thirds rule applies to all special taxes. He said that the two-thirds vote requirement dates to the 1849 state Constitution, which required a supermajority vote of state lawmakers to ask voters to borrow money. “The power to tax is (the) government’s most draconian power,” he told CalMatters. “The people of the state of California have made it a policy that when you are going to exercise that power, it should require a higher degree of consensus.” But opponents say the initiative risks kneecapping funding for local services. Darrell Roberts, president of the California Professional Firefighters union, which represents 38,000 firefighters, called Prop. 43 an insurmountable roadblock (https://www.marinij.com/2026/10/03/opinion-prop-43-sacrifices-local-public-safety-to-protect-corporate-profits/) to raising money for community services. This November, Los Angeles voters will decide on a half-cent sales tax (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-06/lapd-union-will-oppose-half-cent-sales-tax-hike-pushed-by-firefighters-union) proposal to hire more firefighters, Roberts noted. “Under Prop. 43, it’s clear that the powerful few would be protected at the expense of everyone else,” he wrote in the Marin Independent Journal. Supporters have poured almost $15 million into the measure, nearly $10 million of it from the California Business Roundtable PAC. Opponents have collected $6 million, with the biggest contribution, $1.5 million, from a PAC affiliated with the Service Employees International Union of California. Sign up for free Δ Prop. 43 originated from L.A.’s ‘mansion tax’ fight Prop. 43 stems from a bitter fight over Los Angeles’ “mansion tax,” a 4% tax on real estate sales of more than $5.3 million and 5.5% on sales more than $10.6 million. The tax rates rise with inflation. It has generated $1.4 billion (https://housing.lacity.gov/ula-revenue) in revenue since it became law in 2023, according to the city. The tax angered real estate developers (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/04/proposition-realty-mansion-tax-jarvis/) and business groups, who said it impeded new construction of all kinds of developments, including affordable housing. The opposition fueled a campaign led by Coupal’s group earlier this year to qualify a ballot measure that would have slashed real estate sales taxes statewide, applied the two-thirds vote requirement to all special taxes and revoked taxes that previously passed by a simple majority, such as the mansion tax. Prop. 43 is a more modest proposal resulting from an eleventh-hour negotiation between Coupal and Democratic leaders in the state Legislature to kill the more extensive version. Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/buffy-wicks-165044), an Oakland Democrat, authored the compromise language (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260aca22). The measure is limited to the vote threshold and does not apply retroactively to taxes such as the mansion tax. Just days after the Legislature placed Prop. 43 on the ballot, Wicks said she is “adamantly opposed” to it. “The clock was running out, and we had a choice to make: Leave a retroactive measure on the ballot that threatened billions in local funding, or accept a much narrower constitutional amendment that I still believed was bad policy,” Wicks said (https://bsky.app/profile/buffywicks.bsky.social/post/3mpi3t4tkmp2h) in a social media post. Is there public appetite? This isn’t Coupal’s first rodeo. In 2024, his group sponsored a much broader ballot measure to make it harder to raise taxes, but the California Supreme Court unanimously blocked (https://calmatters.org/politics/2024/06/california-taxes-supreme-court-ballot/) it before the election, deeming it an illegal attempt to change the state’s constitution. How will a narrower Prop. 43 perform this year? A September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) from the nonpartisan Public Policy Institute of California found 51% of likely voters would vote no on Prop. 43, versus just 43% who would vote yes. But Coupal hopes the proposal taps into voters’ concerns about affordability and their frustration with the high cost of living in California. “We are in a general climate right now where Californians really feel overtaxed,” he said. “California needs to prioritize its spending before it asks for more.” READ NEXT Why are out-of-state billionaires funding a California voter ID measure? In 2022, 58% of Los Angeles city voters approved a hefty tax on mansion sales. In 2024, 62% of Sonoma County voters backed a half-cent sales tax to fund wildfire response and other emergency services. Neither would have become law under the threshold set by Proposition 43 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/), which would require a two-thirds vote to pass any local tax measures that pay for specific services. Anti-tax advocates such as the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, which helped get Prop. 43 on the ballot, say it should be harder (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/california-constitution-proposition-43-taxes/) to tax Californians in a state where tax rates are already high. They argue that the measure would apply an equal standard to whoever wants a special tax, whether the government or citizen groups. Californians voted in 1996 (https://lao.ca.gov/1996/120196_prop_218/understanding_prop218_1296.html) to establish a two-thirds threshold for special tax measures. For decades, it was widely assumed that the threshold applied to all special taxes — until 2017, when the state Supreme Court said (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2017/08/state-supreme-court-made-easier-raise-taxes/) the law specifically applied only to tax measures put on the ballot by local officials. But what about special taxes proposed by citizens? The court declined to clarify (https://calmatters.org/economy/2019/02/local-tax-chaos-california-supreme-court/). Confusion ensued. Since then, several high-profile local special tax measures placed on the ballot by nongovernmental groups have passed with a simple majority. Local government officials, labor unions and affordable housing advocates oppose the measure, arguing the proposal would make it difficult to collect revenues for essential services, such as firefighting, education and healthcare. They argue it would allow “minority rule (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/proposition-43-taxes-minority-rule/)” because it would only take a third of voters to block special taxes. Jon Coupal, president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, said Prop. 43 would clarify that the two-thirds rule applies to all special taxes. He said that the two-thirds vote requirement dates to the 1849 state Constitution, which required a supermajority vote of state lawmakers to ask voters to borrow money. “The power to tax is (the) government’s most draconian power,” he told CalMatters. “The people of the state of California have made it a policy that when you are going to exercise that power, it should require a higher degree of consensus.” But opponents say the initiative risks kneecapping funding for local services. Darrell Roberts, president of the California Professional Firefighters union, which represents 38,000 firefighters, called Prop. 43 an insurmountable roadblock (https://www.marinij.com/2026/10/03/opinion-prop-43-sacrifices-local-public-safety-to-protect-corporate-profits/) to raising money for community services. This November, Los Angeles voters will decide on a half-cent sales tax (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-06/lapd-union-will-oppose-half-cent-sales-tax-hike-pushed-by-firefighters-union) proposal to hire more firefighters, Roberts noted. “Under Prop. 43, it’s clear that the powerful few would be protected at the expense of everyone else,” he wrote in the Marin Independent Journal. Supporters have poured almost $15 million into the measure, nearly $10 million of it from the California Business Roundtable PAC. Opponents have collected $6 million, with the biggest contribution, $1.5 million, from a PAC affiliated with the Service Employees International Union of California. The tax rates rise with inflation. It has generated $1.4 billion (https://housing.lacity.gov/ula-revenue) in revenue since it became law in 2023, according to the city. The tax angered real estate developers (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/04/proposition-realty-mansion-tax-jarvis/) and business groups, who said it impeded new construction of all kinds of developments, including affordable housing. The opposition fueled a campaign led by Coupal’s group earlier this year to qualify a ballot measure that would have slashed real estate sales taxes statewide, applied the two-thirds vote requirement to all special taxes and revoked taxes that previously passed by a simple majority, such as the mansion tax. Prop. 43 is a more modest proposal resulting from an eleventh-hour negotiation between Coupal and Democratic leaders in the state Legislature to kill the more extensive version. Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/buffy-wicks-165044), an Oakland Democrat, authored the compromise language (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260aca22). The measure is limited to the vote threshold and does not apply retroactively to taxes such as the mansion tax. Just days after the Legislature placed Prop. 43 on the ballot, Wicks said she is “adamantly opposed” to it. “The clock was running out, and we had a choice to make: Leave a retroactive measure on the ballot that threatened billions in local funding, or accept a much narrower constitutional amendment that I still believed was bad policy,” Wicks said (https://bsky.app/profile/buffywicks.bsky.social/post/3mpi3t4tkmp2h) in a social media post. Is there public appetite? This isn’t Coupal’s first rodeo. In 2024, his group sponsored a much broader ballot measure to make it harder to raise taxes, but the California Supreme Court unanimously blocked (https://calmatters.org/politics/2024/06/california-taxes-supreme-court-ballot/) it before the election, deeming it an illegal attempt to change the state’s constitution. How will a narrower Prop. 43 perform this year? A September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) from the nonpartisan Public Policy Institute of California found 51% of likely voters would vote no on Prop. 43, versus just 43% who would vote yes. Schaben, Los Angeles Times via Getty Images In summary The measure would require two-thirds of voters to approve any local special taxes, instead of the simple majority for citizen-led initiatives. Anti-tax advocates say it should be that hard for governments to tax Californians, but local officials say it could constrain funding for essential services. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. In 2022, 58% of Los Angeles city voters approved a hefty tax on mansion sales. In 2024, 62% of Sonoma County voters backed a half-cent sales tax to fund wildfire response and other emergency services. Neither would have become law under the threshold set by Proposition 43 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/), which would require a two-thirds vote to pass any local tax measures that pay for specific services. Anti-tax advocates such as the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, which helped get Prop. 43 on the ballot, say it should be harder (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/california-constitution-proposition-43-taxes/) to tax Californians in a state where tax rates are already high. They argue that the measure would apply an equal standard to whoever wants a special tax, whether the government or citizen groups. Californians voted in 1996 (https://lao.ca.gov/1996/120196_prop_218/understanding_prop218_1296.html) to establish a two-thirds threshold for special tax measures. For decades, it was widely assumed that the threshold applied to all special taxes — until 2017, when the state Supreme Court said (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2017/08/state-supreme-court-made-easier-raise-taxes/) the law specifically applied only to tax measures put on the ballot by local officials. But what about special taxes proposed by citizens? The court declined to clarify (https://calmatters.org/economy/2019/02/local-tax-chaos-california-supreme-court/). Confusion ensued. Since then, several high-profile local special tax measures placed on the ballot by nongovernmental groups have passed with a simple majority. Local government officials, labor unions and affordable housing advocates oppose the measure, arguing the proposal would make it difficult to collect revenues for essential services, such as firefighting, education and healthcare. They argue it would allow “minority rule (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/proposition-43-taxes-minority-rule/)” because it would only take a third of voters to block special taxes. Jon Coupal, president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, said Prop. 43 would clarify that the two-thirds rule applies to all special taxes. He said that the two-thirds vote requirement dates to the 1849 state Constitution, which required a supermajority vote of state lawmakers to ask voters to borrow money. “The power to tax is (the) government’s most draconian power,” he told CalMatters. “The people of the state of California have made it a policy that when you are going to exercise that power, it should require a higher degree of consensus.” But opponents say the initiative risks kneecapping funding for local services. Darrell Roberts, president of the California Professional Firefighters union, which represents 38,000 firefighters, called Prop. 43 an insurmountable roadblock (https://www.marinij.com/2026/10/03/opinion-prop-43-sacrifices-local-public-safety-to-protect-corporate-profits/) to raising money for community services. This November, Los Angeles voters will decide on a half-cent sales tax (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-06/lapd-union-will-oppose-half-cent-sales-tax-hike-pushed-by-firefighters-union) proposal to hire more firefighters, Roberts noted. “Under Prop. 43, it’s clear that the powerful few would be protected at the expense of everyone else,” he wrote in the Marin Independent Journal. Supporters have poured almost $15 million into the measure, nearly $10 million of it from the California Business Roundtable PAC. Opponents have collected $6 million, with the biggest contribution, $1.5 million, from a PAC affiliated with the Service Employees International Union of California. Sign up for free Δ Prop. 43 originated from L.A.’s ‘mansion tax’ fight Prop. 43 stems from a bitter fight over Los Angeles’ “mansion tax,” a 4% tax on real estate sales of more than $5.3 million and 5.5% on sales more than $10.6 million. The tax rates rise with inflation. It has generated $1.4 billion (https://housing.lacity.gov/ula-revenue) in revenue since it became law in 2023, according to the city. The tax angered real estate developers (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/04/proposition-realty-mansion-tax-jarvis/) and business groups, who said it impeded new construction of all kinds of developments, including affordable housing. The opposition fueled a campaign led by Coupal’s group earlier this year to qualify a ballot measure that would have slashed real estate sales taxes statewide, applied the two-thirds vote requirement to all special taxes and revoked taxes that previously passed by a simple majority, such as the mansion tax. Prop. 43 is a more modest proposal resulting from an eleventh-hour negotiation between Coupal and Democratic leaders in the state Legislature to kill the more extensive version. Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/buffy-wicks-165044), an Oakland Democrat, authored the compromise language (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260aca22). The measure is limited to the vote threshold and does not apply retroactively to taxes such as the mansion tax. Just days after the Legislature placed Prop. 43 on the ballot, Wicks said she is “adamantly opposed” to it. “The clock was running out, and we had a choice to make: Leave a retroactive measure on the ballot that threatened billions in local funding, or accept a much narrower constitutional amendment that I still believed was bad policy,” Wicks said (https://bsky.app/profile/buffywicks.bsky.social/post/3mpi3t4tkmp2h) in a social media post. Is there public appetite? This isn’t Coupal’s first rodeo. In 2024, his group sponsored a much broader ballot measure to make it harder to raise taxes, but the California Supreme Court unanimously blocked (https://calmatters.org/politics/2024/06/california-taxes-supreme-court-ballot/) it before the election, deeming it an illegal attempt to change the state’s constitution. How will a narrower Prop. 43 perform this year? A September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) from the nonpartisan Public Policy Institute of California found 51% of likely voters would vote no on Prop. 43, versus just 43% who would vote yes. But Coupal hopes the proposal taps into voters’ concerns about affordability and their frustration with the high cost of living in California. “We are in a general climate right now where Californians really feel overtaxed,” he said. “California needs to prioritize its spending before it asks for more.” READ NEXT Why are out-of-state billionaires funding a California voter ID measure?
